Surah al-Nasr is Medinan and has three verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿When the help of Allah and the victory come,﴾ ﴿and you see people entering the religion of Allah in multitudes,﴾ ﴿then glorify your Lord with His praise and seek His forgiveness. Indeed, He is ever Accepting of repentance.﴾

This surah is Medinan. It was revealed as the Prophet (ﷺ) was returning from the expedition of Khaybar, and he lived two years after its revelation. Ibn Umar said: it was revealed in the middle of the days of tashriq (ayyam al-tashriq) at Mina during the Farewell Pilgrimage, and he lived after it eighty days or so. (ﷺ). Since in His saying, ﴿To you is your religion, and to me is mine﴾ [al-Kafirun: 6] there is a form of truce, in this surah there came what indicates their intimidation and threat, and that the coming of Allah's help, the conquest of Makkah, the collapse of the creed of idols, and the manifestation of the religion of Allah the Exalted had arrived.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "idha" is in the accusative governed by "sabbih," and it refers to the future, and the announcement of that before it happened is one of the signs of prophethood. End quote. Al-Hawfi said likewise. It is not correct for "fasabbih" to govern "idha" because of the fa', since the fa' in the answer of the conditional does not allow the verb after it to govern the conditional noun; rather, the governing element in "idha" is the verb that follows it, according to the sound and established view in Arabic grammar. We have argued for this in our commentary on al-Tashil and elsewhere, even though the well-known view is otherwise. "Al-nasr" means aid and manifestation against the enemy, and "al-fath" means the conquest of lands. The object of "al-nasr" and "al-fath" is omitted. The apparent meaning is the help of His Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers over their enemies, and the conquest of Makkah and other places over them, such as al-Ta'if, the cities of the Hijaz, and much of Yemen. It has been said: his (ﷺ) victory over Quraysh and the conquest of Makkah, which took place on the tenth of Ramadan in the eighth year (AH), with him, peace be upon him, accompanied by ten thousand of the Muhajirun and the Ansar.

The majority read ﴿yadkhulun﴾ in the active voice, while Ibn Kathir in one narration read it in the passive voice.

﴿in the religion of Allah﴾ in the creed of Islam, to which no other religion may be added. ﴿in multitudes﴾ meaning large groups: a whole tribe would enter it together, after they had been entering it one by one and two by two.

Al-Hasan said: When he (ﷺ) conquered Makkah, the Arabs turned to one another and said: as for victory over the people of the Sanctuary, there are no means for it, for Allah had protected them from the companions of the Elephant. Abu Umar ibn Abd al-Barr said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not die while there was a disbelieving man among the Arabs; rather, all entered Islam after Hunayn, some by coming themselves and some by sending their delegations. Ibn Atiyyah said: The intended meaning, and Allah knows best, is the Arabs who were idol-worshippers. As for the Christians of Banu Taghlib, I do not think they ever embraced Islam during the lifetime of the Messenger (ﷺ), but they paid the jizyah. Muqatil and Ikrimah said: the intended people are the people of Yemen, of whom seven hundred men came as a delegation. The majority said: the delegations of the Arabs, and their entry took place between the conquest of Makkah and his death (ﷺ). "Afwajan" is the plural of "fawj." Al-Hawfi said: its regular plural would be "afwuj," but the damma was considered heavy on the waw, so it was changed to "afwaj." It is as if he meant that it should have been a doubled-middle-radical-free (sound-middle) form like its sound counterpart, so that just as the regular plural of a sound-middle form of fa'l is af'ul and not af'al, so too this would be; but the matter in this defective-middle form is the reverse: the regular plural is af'al, as in hawd and ahwad, and af'ul is rare in it, as in thawb and athwub. "Afwajan" is a circumstantial accusative (hal), and "yadkhulun" is a circumstantial clause or a second object if "ara'ayta" means "you knew," which takes two objects. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is either a circumstantial accusative, on the basis that "ara'ayta" means "you saw" or "you recognized." End quote. We do not know of "ra'ayta" being used in the sense of "you recognized," so in that we would need to verify it.

﴿So glorify your Lord with His praise﴾ meaning: while joined with His praise for these blessings which He bestowed upon you, of your victory over the enemies, your conquest of lands, and the Islam of the people. What blessing is greater than this? For every good deed that the Muslims perform is recorded in his scale.

From Aisha: The Prophet (ﷺ) used to say much before his death: "Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You. I seek Your forgiveness and turn to You in repentance." Al-Zamakhshari said: The command to seek forgiveness together with glorification completes the command regarding that which is the foundation of the religion, namely combining obedience with guarding against disobedience; and so that his being commanded to do so, despite his infallibility, would be a kindness to his community. Also, seeking forgiveness is part of humility and self-abasement, so it is itself an act of worship.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed, I seek forgiveness from Allah a hundred times in a day and a night." End quote. He himself understood from this surah the nearness of his end. When he (ﷺ) recited it to them, the Companions rejoiced, but al-Abbas wept. He said: "What makes you weep, uncle?" He said: "Your soul has been announced to you." He said: "Indeed, it is as you say." He lived two years after it.

﴿Indeed, He is ever Accepting of repentance﴾: in it is a great hope for those who seek forgiveness.
